companyCaseStudy.title: How Twitter Scaled Timeline Fanout to Serve ~500M Tweets/Day and Get Reads Under 150ms
companyCaseStudy.summary: Twitter needed to serve millions of users a realtime home timeline with sub-100ms perceived latency while hundreds of millions of new Tweets arrived daily. The engineering answer blended fanout-on-write, targeted fanout-on-read for celebrities, a multi-tenant low-latency storage (Manhattan), and aggressive caching—cutting read latency from seconds to ~100ms at peak.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook

Twitter ingests on the order of hundreds of millions of Tweets per day (commonly quoted ~500M/day at peak eras). That’s a steady stream of new objects that must be visible to followers immediately—while reads (users fetching their home timelines) outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. The naive approach quickly turns into a write explosion: 1 Tweet × 100 followers = 100 writes if you push a copy to each follower’s timeline.

---

## Problem — the timeline paradox

- Scale: hundreds of millions of Tweets/day; millions of active timelines being read constantly.
- Requirement: timeline reads must feel instant (sub-100–200ms tail latencies) for a good UX.
- Economics: you can optimize reads or writes, but each choice has costs—write amplification, storage bloat, or read complexity and latency.

### Why this is hard

Reads are far more frequent than writes. Users expect their timelines to show new content instantly. If you store a single canonical Tweet and compute each user’s timeline on read (fanout-on-read), you face complex, high-latency merges and heavy backend work on every view. If you instead fanout-on-write (precompute timeline entries for every follower), writes multiply by the follower-count and storage grows dramatically.

## Challenge — varied follower distributions and spikes

- Most users have small follower counts; some celebrities have millions.
- A one-size-fits-all fanout strategy either wastes resources (full fanout for celebrities) or increases read latency (compute heavy fanout-on-read for normal users).
- Significant peaks (breaking news, viral Tweets) cause sudden write/read surges.

## Twitter’s solution (high-level story)

Twitter adopted a hybrid approach:

1. Fanout-on-write for the common case (users with modest follower counts). On write, background workers push lightweight timeline entries into per-user timeline stores.
2. Fanout-on-read for very large follower counts (celebrities / broadcast accounts) to avoid writing millions of copies up-front.
3. Very low-latency multi-tenant storage (Manhattan) to store precomputed timeline shards and serve reads at low latency.
4. Aggressive caching at the edge (memcached / Twemproxy / CDN) to serve most reads without touching the backing store.
5. Backpressure, batching, and durable queues for fanout workers so viral events don’t collapse the system.

### Architecture (simplified)

```mermaid
graph LR
  Producer[Tweet Producer] --> Ingest[Ingest Layer (Hose, Kafka)]
  Ingest --> FanoutWorker[Fanout Workers]
  FanoutWorker --> Manhattan[Manhattan (Per-user timeline shards)]
  FanoutWorker --> DurableQueue[Durable Queue / Retry]
  Manhattan --> Cache[Memcache / Edge Cache]
  Client --> CDN[CDN / Edge]
  CDN --> Cache
  CDN --> API[Front-end API Layer]
  API --> Cache
  API --> Manhattan
  CelebAccount[High-follower Accounts] -.-> API
  CelebAccount -.-> FanoutOnRead[Fanout-on-Read Path]
```

- Normal users: Tweet ingestion -> fanout workers -> write small timeline entries into Manhattan (partitioned by user id) -> reads served from memcache or Manhattan.
- High-follower accounts: ingest the Tweet but mark it for fanout-on-read. Reads merge the recent celebrity Tweets on the fly (small, targeted work) instead of writing millions of timeline rows.

### Flow (write path)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  T[Tweet arrives] --> Q[Write to durable queue]
  Q --> W[Fanout worker pool]
  W -->|Batch & partition| P[Per-user timeline shards]
  P --> M[Persist to Manhattan]
  M --> C[Invalidate/Update edge cache]
```

## Key implementation details and tradeoffs

- Storage: Fanout-on-write increases storage (write amplification). Twitter accepted ~N× storage growth because it yielded much lower read latency—reads dominated cost/perf.
- Sharding: timelines were sharded by user id so that fanout workers could partition work and push updates independently.
- Batching & backpressure: workers batch writes per destination shard and use durable queues; if consumers lag, the system applies rate limits and offers degraded freshness rather than collapse.
- Hybrid fanout: accounts above a follower threshold are white-listed for fanout-on-read to avoid writing millions of copies. This threshold is tuned over time.
- Cache hierarchy: most reads are served from the edge cache (memcache / CDN). Manhattan is the low-latency persistent store when cache misses occur.

## Before vs After (approximate, representative numbers)

| Metric | Before (heavy fanout-on-read / naive) | After (hybrid fanout-on-write + cache) |
|--------|----------------------------------------:|----------------------------------------:|
| Tweets/day (ingest) | 500M | 500M |
| Average reads/sec | large, spiky | same, but served from cache |
| Read latency (p95) | ~1.5s (compute + merge) | ~100–150ms (cache + Manhattan fallback) |
| Cache hit rate | ~60% | ~95–98% |
| Storage cost (timeline rows) | Lower | Higher (write amplification, e.g., ~5–10×) |
| User perceived freshness | Slower for reads | Near-instant for most users |

> Note: exact numbers varied over time and by internal era. Table shows typical tradeoffs Twitter documented and engineers discussed publicly: winning on latency required accepting write amplification and more storage.

## Results & operational wins

- Read latencies collapsed from second-scale merges to ~100ms for the vast majority of users, producing a much snappier timeline.
- Cache-first reads reduced load on core storage by an order of magnitude; Manhattan provided durable low-latency fallback.
- Hybrid fanout prevented blowup for celebrity accounts while keeping normal users’ timelines prepopulated.
- Backpressure and durable queues turned viral storms from live outages into manageable background workloads.

## Lessons learned (from Twitter’s experience)

- Optimize for the common case: most users have modest follower counts and benefit from precomputed timelines.
- Use hybrid strategies: fanout-on-write + fanout-on-read gives the best of both worlds when follower distribution is heavy-tailed.
- Accept some costs (storage, write amplification) to massively reduce read latency and backend complexity.
- Protect the system with batching, backpressure, and retry queues: reliability matters as much as design.

## Anecdote — the celebrity problem

One well-known operational pain: a single celebrity Tweet could imply millions of writes in fanout-on-write. Twitter solved it by detecting high-follower accounts and switching to a fanout-on-read approach for them; that kept writes reasonable while allowing reads to merge a small list of celebrity updates on demand. This hybridization was instrumental in keeping the whole system stable under viral loads.

---

## Diagrams recap

- Architecture: precompute timelines into Manhattan, cache heavily at the edge, hybrid fanout for large accounts.
- Flow: durable queue → fanout workers → per-user shards → cache invalidation → read path.
keyTakeaways: Hybrid fanout (on-write for normal users, on-read for huge accounts) balances latency vs storage — yield: p95 read latency cut from ~1.5s to ~100–150ms for most users.
Optimize for read-heavy workloads by precomputing where follower counts are modest; accept write amplification (storage increase often 5–10×) in exchange for massive read latency wins.
Protect fanout with batching, durable queues, and backpressure so viral events degrade gracefully rather than crash the system.

concept.title: Stop the Cascade: The Circuit Breaker Pattern for Resilient Services
concept.summary: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by automatically stopping calls to unhealthy dependencies and giving them time to recover. They convert noisy retries and slow failure paths into predictable, observable behavior with clear fallbacks.
keyTakeaways: Circuit breakers stop cascading failures by short‑circuiting calls to unhealthy dependencies and providing controlled recovery (half‑open trials).
Tune thresholds and timeouts using real metrics; avoid naive defaults and protect against thundering‑herd on recovery.
Combine breakers with timeouts, retries (capped + backoff), rate limiting, and observability for robust behavior.
